questions.q: What's the difference between a paginated report (SSRS) and an interactive Power BI report?
options: Paginated reports are designed for fixed-layout, printable/exportable output even across many pages; Power BI is built for interactive on-screen exploration
They're the same technology with different names
Paginated reports can't be parameterized
Power BI reports can be exported to RDL files natively
questions.explain: SSRS paginated reports are purpose-built for precise, page-by-page layouts that print and export cleanly, like invoices and statements — a very different design goal from Power BI's interactive, on-screen analytical canvas.

questions.q: What file extension does an SSRS report definition use?
options: .rdl
.pbix
.rpt
.ssrs
questions.explain: SSRS reports are defined in RDL, Report Definition Language, an XML-based format saved as a .rdl file.

questions.q: What is a Tablix in SSRS?
options: The unified data region that can render as a table, matrix, or list depending on its row/column groupings
A type of database index
A scheduling component
A chart-only visual
questions.explain: Tablix is SSRS's single, flexible data region — the same underlying control becomes a simple table, a cross-tab matrix, or a list purely based on how you configure its row and column groups.

questions.q: What's the purpose of a Dataset in Report Builder/SSDT, separate from a Data Source?
options: A Data Source defines the connection; a Dataset defines the actual query/fields that populate a specific region of the report
They're interchangeable terms for the same object
A Dataset always requires its own separate Data Source
Datasets can only return a single row
questions.explain: The Data Source holds connection info like server and credentials; a Dataset sits on top of it and defines the actual query and the resulting field list that a Tablix or chart binds to.

questions.q: What does a Group in a Tablix let you do that a plain flat table can't?
options: Roll rows up by a shared value, with subtotals/headers per group, like GROUP BY for the report layout itself
Change the report's page size
Add a parameter
Connect to a second data source
questions.explain: Grouping in a Tablix is what turns a flat row list into a structured report — rows collapse under a shared key, with the option to show group headers, subtotals, and even collapse/expand behavior.

questions.q: What does making an SSRS parameter "multi-value" allow the report to do?
options: Let the user select more than one value at once, typically used with an IN() condition in the underlying query
Accept only numeric input
Automatically hide the parameter
Force the report to run without any filter
questions.explain: A multi-value parameter presents a checklist to the user instead of a single dropdown, and the selected values are passed into the dataset query as a collection — usually consumed with WHERE Column IN (@Param).

questions.q: What's a "cascading parameter" setup in SSRS?
options: A parameter's available values are filtered based on the value already chosen in an earlier parameter, such as State filtering which Cities appear
A parameter that changes color when selected
A parameter that runs multiple reports at once
A required parameter with no default
questions.explain: Cascading parameters chain together — choosing State re-runs the City parameter's own dataset filtered to that State, so the next dropdown only shows relevant options.

questions.q: What's the effect of setting a parameter's "Allow blank value" versus giving it a Default value?
options: Allow blank value lets the user submit an empty string; a Default value pre-fills the parameter so the report can run without the user picking anything
They do the same thing
Default value disables the parameter entirely
Allow blank value is only available for date parameters
questions.explain: These solve different problems — a default pre-populates a parameter's value so the report can render immediately without user interaction, while "allow blank" specifically permits an empty string as a valid, distinct submitted value.

questions.q: In an SSRS expression, what does the syntax =Fields!SalesAmount.Value refer to?
options: The value of the SalesAmount field from the report's current row/dataset
A global report variable
A parameter named SalesAmount
A built-in aggregate function
questions.explain: Fields!<FieldName>.Value is SSRS expression syntax for reading a dataset field's value in the current row context — the fundamental building block of nearly every SSRS expression.

questions.q: How would you conditionally color a text box red only when its value is negative, using an SSRS expression?
options: Use an IIF expression in the color property, such as =IIF(Fields!Amount.Value < 0, "Red", "Black")
Manually recolor the cell in Report Builder for every possible value
It's not possible without custom code
Use a separate report for negative values
questions.explain: SSRS supports expression-driven formatting on almost every property, including Color — IIF() is the standard inline-conditional pattern for exactly this kind of conditional formatting.

questions.q: What does the built-in field =Globals!PageNumber & " of " & Globals!TotalPages typically render in a page footer?
options: Something like "3 of 12" — the current page number and total page count
The report's file name
The date the report was last modified
The number of rows in the dataset
questions.explain: Globals!PageNumber and Globals!TotalPages are built-in SSRS globals meant specifically for footers, giving a running "page X of Y" display as the report paginates.

questions.q: What's required before an SSRS chart can plot any data?
options: At least one Category field and one Value/Series field mapped from the underlying dataset
A minimum of 3 datasets
A parameter
A subscription
questions.explain: Every SSRS chart needs, at minimum, a category, such as Month, on the axis, and a value/series, such as Revenue, pulled from a dataset before it has anything to draw.

questions.q: What's a Gauge data region typically used for in SSRS?
options: Showing a single value against a range or target, like a speedometer-style KPI indicator
Displaying tabular row-level detail
Running a subscription schedule
Connecting to a second data source
questions.explain: Gauges are single-value visual indicators, linear or radial, purpose-built for KPI-style "how does this one number compare to its target/range" displays, distinct from the row-level Tablix/chart data regions.

questions.q: What's a Drillthrough report in SSRS?
options: A separate report that a user navigates to by clicking a value in the original report, typically passing that value as a parameter
A report that automatically refreshes every few seconds
A report with no parameters
A chart type
questions.explain: Drillthrough links a cell/value in one report to an entirely separate report, passing the clicked value along as a parameter — e.g. clicking a customer name opens that customer's detail report.

questions.q: What's the difference between Drillthrough and Drilldown, i.e. toggle show/hide, in SSRS?
options: Drilldown expands/collapses detail rows within the same report; Drillthrough navigates to a completely different report
They're the same feature under two names
Drilldown requires a subscription; Drillthrough doesn't
Drillthrough can only work with charts
questions.explain: Drilldown, via a group's ToggleItem, reveals or hides detail rows in place, within the same Tablix — Drillthrough leaves the current report entirely and opens a different one, usually with a parameter passed along.

questions.q: What's a Data-Driven Subscription used for in SSRS?
options: Delivering a report to a dynamic, data-driven list of recipients/parameters, such as emailing each region's manager their own filtered version
Scheduling a report to run once, with the same output for everyone
Encrypting subscription emails
Only exporting to Excel
questions.explain: A standard subscription has one fixed set of parameters and recipients; a data-driven subscription pulls its recipient list and per-recipient parameter values from a query — so 50 regional managers can each automatically get their own filtered report.

questions.q: Which export format would you choose to preserve exact page layout and pagination for printing?
options: PDF
CSV
XML
A data feed (.atomsvc)
questions.explain: PDF renders SSRS's fixed page layout and pagination exactly as designed — CSV, XML, and data feeds are for exporting the underlying data, not preserving the visual report layout.

questions.q: What's the role of the Report Server, in native mode, at runtime?
options: It hosts and serves RDL-based paginated reports for on-demand viewing, scheduling, and subscriptions
Report Server is only used during report design, not at runtime
Power BI Report Server can't host paginated reports at all
They require completely different report file formats
questions.explain: The Report Server, whether SQL Server Reporting Services or Power BI Report Server, is the runtime host — it's what actually renders reports on demand, runs schedules, and delivers subscriptions once a report is deployed to it.

questions.q: What does setting row-level or item-level security on a Report Server folder control?
options: Which users/roles can view, run, or manage specific reports and folders
Which columns appear in a report's dataset
The report's page orientation
The report's refresh schedule
questions.explain: Report Server security is applied at the folder/item level in the catalog — it governs who can browse to, run, edit, or manage a given report, separately from anything in the report's own query logic.

questions.q: When building a capstone paginated report for a Microsoft BI stack, why would you point its dataset at the data warehouse rather than the raw OLTP source tables?
options: The warehouse's dimensional model is already shaped for fast, simple reporting queries — joining raw OLTP tables would be slower and more complex
SSRS can't connect to OLTP databases at all
Raw OLTP tables don't support parameters
It's required by SSRS licensing
questions.explain: A star-schema warehouse is built specifically so reporting queries are simple, fast joins from a fact table to a handful of dimensions — querying live OLTP tables directly for reporting tends to mean more complex joins and risks competing with transactional workload.
